summary: This unit examines the impacts of desertification on ecosystem services, biodiversity, and socio-economic systems, including human health, energy infrastructure, and migration. It also evaluates management practices such as integrated crop-soil-water management, grazing and fire management, and bush encroachment clearance.

passages.text: Land-use changes often lead to reductions in SOC and organic matter inputs into soil, increasing soil salinity and soil erosion. In addition to the loss of soil, erosion reduces soil nutrients and organic matter, thereby impacting land’s productive capacity.

Precipitation, by affecting soil moisture content, is considered to be the principal determinant of the capacity of drylands to sequester carbon. Low soil water availability promotes soil microbial respiration, yet there is insufficient moisture to stimulate plant productivity, resulting in net carbon emissions at an ecosystem level.

Soil erosion by wind results in a loss of fine soil particles (silt and clay), reducing the ability of soil to sequester carbon. Moreover, dust storms reduce crop yields by loss of plant tissue caused by sandblasting, exposing crop roots, crop seed burial under sand deposits, and leading to losses of nutrients and fertiliser from topsoil.

heading_path: 3.4.1.2 Impacts on biodiversity: Plant and wildlife
passages.text: Increasing aridity exacerbates the risk of extinction of some plant species, especially those that are already threatened due to small populations or restricted habitats.

At the local level, on the other hand, there is limited evidence and high agreement that desertification increased multidimensional poverty. For example, Diao and Sarpong (2011) estimated that land degradation lowered agricultural incomes in Ghana by 4.2 billion USD between 2006 and 2015, increasing the national poverty rate by 5.4% in 2015.

heading_path: 3.4.2.2 Impacts on food and nutritional insecurity
passages.text: The major mechanism through which climate change and desertification affect food security is through their impacts on agricultural productivity. There is robust evidence pointing to negative impacts of climate change on crop yields in dryland areas (high agreement).

heading_path: 3.4.2.5 Impacts on water scarcity and use
passages.text: Reduced water retention capacity of degraded soils amplifies floods, reinforces degradation processes through soil erosion, and reduces annual intake of water to aquifers, exacerbating existing water scarcities.

Compared to conventional (flood or furrow) irrigation, drip irrigation methods are more efficient in supplying water to the plant root zone, resulting in lower water requirements and enhanced water use efficiency (robust evidence, high agreement).

The adoption of intercropping (inter – and intra-row planting of companion crops) and relay cropping (temporally differentiated planting of companion crops) maintains soil cover over a larger fraction of the year, leading to an increase in production, soil nitrogen, species diversity and a decrease in pest abundance (robust evidence, medium agreement).

heading_path: 3.6.1.2 Grazing and fire management in drylands
passages.text: Rangeland management systems such as sustainable grazing approaches and re-vegetation increase rangeland productivity (high confidence).
